AI VIDEO WORKFLOW · UPDATED 2026

How to Make AI Videos for Free in 2026

Written by Ashok Kumar Yadav

Xenors founder and technical writer. View author profile · Editorial policy · How we verify

A practical workflow for turning an idea into short AI-generated clips, narration, captions and a finished YouTube or Instagram video—without pretending every “free” tool is unlimited.

By Ashok Kumar Yadav, founder of Xenors and backend developer · Published November 7, 2026 · Last updated November 7, 2026

Quick answer: the simplest free AI video stack

For a beginner, a practical stack is ChatGPT for the script and prompts, Google Flow or Adobe Firefly for short generated clips, and Microsoft Clipchamp for editing and export. Google Flow currently gives non-subscribers 50 Flow credits per day; Firefly has limited free daily generations; Clipchamp's free personal plan exports up to 1080p without adding a watermark when you stay within free features. These limits can change, so check the official plan pages before a large project.

What “free AI video” really means in 2026

Free rarely means unlimited. Most AI video services use one of three models: a small daily allowance, a one-time pool of credits, or limited access to selected models. The output can also differ by resolution, clip length, queue priority, watermark policy and commercial-use rights. That is why this guide treats the generator and editor as separate parts of the workflow.

If your goal is a 30-second Reel or Short, you do not need one model to create the entire video. Generate four to six short scenes, keep the best takes, then assemble them in an editor. This makes it easier to fix a bad hand, an inconsistent face or a flickering object without regenerating the whole project.

Step 1: choose one video idea and one audience

Start with a single outcome. “Make an AI video” is too broad; “make a 30-second YouTube Short explaining what a Mars morning might look like” is concrete. Decide the viewer, platform, length and tone before you write prompts. This gives every later scene a reason to exist.

A useful brief is: topic + viewer + platform + duration + promise. Example: “Beginner audience, YouTube Short, 35 seconds, show five visual moments from a future Mars settlement and end with one question.”

Step 2: write the script with ChatGPT

Use ChatGPT as a planning and writing assistant rather than expecting it to render the entire finished video. Ask for a hook, narration and a shot description for every scene. Keep each spoken line short enough to fit the shot.

Prompt:

Write a 35-second YouTube Short about a morning on Mars. Audience: curious beginners. Start with a two-second hook. Divide the script into six scenes. For each scene give: narration, on-screen text, visual description and a text-to-video prompt. Keep each shot visually simple.

If you already have a blog post, do not paste the full article into a video model. First ask ChatGPT to extract the core idea, then convert that into a sequence of shots.

Related: how to structure reliable ChatGPT workflows and the Xenors AI hub.

Step 3: turn the script into six simple scenes

Each scene should have one subject, one action and one camera idea. A prompt such as “a robot enters a lab, opens a door, picks up a vial, talks to a scientist and the camera flies outside” asks the model to solve too many continuity problems at once.

Use a repeatable formula: subject + action + environment + framing + camera movement + lighting + style. For example: “Astronaut walks through a compact Mars greenhouse, rows of green plants under white grow lights, medium tracking shot, slow camera movement, realistic documentary style.”

Step 4: generate short clips, not one long video

Generate one scene at a time. For a 30- to 40-second video, six short clips are usually easier to control than one long prompt. Save the prompt and seed/reference settings when the tool exposes them, because consistency becomes harder if you change wording radically between scenes.

If text-to-video struggles to keep a character consistent, create or select one reference image first and use image-to-video for later scenes. Keep clothes, lighting direction and camera distance similar. When a clip fails, change only one variable at a time—for example the hand action or camera movement—so you know what improved the result.

Visual slot: Replace this with a real generator screenshot after you create the sample clip.

Step 5: add voice, captions and audio

You can record your own narration, use a text-to-speech voice you have the right to use, or create a caption-led video with music. The safest workflow is to finish narration first, place it on the timeline, then trim the visual clips to match the spoken pace.

Keep captions short. One or two lines at a time are easier to read than a paragraph. If you use music, choose a licensed track or a platform library with terms that fit your use. Do not clone a real person's voice without permission.

For YouTube, realistic AI-generated or meaningfully altered scenes may require disclosure. YouTube's current help says creators should disclose realistic generated scenes that did not actually occur, and its 2026 update says the label itself does not reduce recommendations or monetization eligibility.

Step 6: edit and export the final video

Put the clips in story order, cut dead time and make the first visual appear immediately. Avoid a logo animation before the hook. Use Clipchamp, Canva or another editor you already trust. If you want a genuinely free final export, verify that every stock asset and effect in the project is included in your plan before you finish.

Complete example: a 30-second Mars AI video

  1. Scene 1 — Hook: “What would your morning look like if you woke up on Mars?” Visual: sunrise over a habitat dome.
  2. Scene 2 — Home: Show a compact habitat interior with a window onto the red landscape. Narration explains pressure and radiation protection.
  3. Scene 3 — Food: Show a hydroponic greenhouse. Narration: fresh food would likely depend on controlled growing systems.
  4. Scene 4 — Travel: Show a pressurized rover crossing a rocky plain. Keep the vehicle movement slow and believable.
  5. Scene 5 — Work: Show two astronauts checking equipment outside the habitat. Narration: every routine task would involve safety procedures.
  6. Scene 6 — Closing + CTA: Wide sunset shot of the settlement. Narration: “Would you live here for a year?” On-screen text repeats the question for comments.

Generate each scene separately, place the narration on the timeline, then trim the visuals to the voice. If one shot looks bad, replace only that shot.

How to make AI videos in Hindi or Hinglish

The generation workflow is the same, but narration and on-screen text need extra attention. Write the story in the language your audience naturally understands, while keeping visual prompts descriptive and literal. If the video model performs better with English visual prompts, that does not mean the narration must be English.

Hindi script prompt:

30 second ki Hindi YouTube Short script likho: “AI se future city kaise dikhegi?” First 2 seconds me strong hook ho. 6 scenes do. Har scene ke liye Hindi narration, short on-screen caption aur detailed English visual prompt do.

Hinglish prompt:

Create a 35-second Hinglish Reel for Indian beginners on “AI video kaise banaye free me”. Keep the narration conversational, not formal Hindi. Give 6 scenes, each with one visual action and a separate English text-to-video prompt.

Caption-cleanup prompt:

Is Hindi/Hinglish narration ko captions ke liye short lines me break karo. Har line maximum 6-8 words ki ho. Meaning change mat karo, unnecessary English words remove karo, aur proper punctuation use karo.

For Hindi captions, use a font that clearly supports Devanagari and check every line manually. Automatic transcription can misread names, English product terms and mixed Hindi-English sentences. Roman Hindi can work for some audiences, but Devanagari is easier to read for others; match the style to your channel instead of mixing scripts randomly.

Keep the first caption visible immediately with the hook. Avoid covering a face with text. If you use English visual prompts, save them below your Hindi script so the scene can be regenerated later without rewriting the creative direction.

Can you really make AI videos without a watermark?

Sometimes, but the answer depends on the tool and plan. Pika currently says outputs on its Free plan are watermark-free, but the same Free plan does not grant commercial rights. Clipchamp says it does not add a watermark to exports; if you use premium assets you cannot export until you remove them or upgrade. Runway states Free-tier generations include watermarks. Google Flow uses invisible SynthID on generated outputs and can apply a visible watermark; its current help specifically notes automatic visible watermarking for users in India, South Korea and Vietnam unless they are on the specified Ultra plan.

Avoid random “watermark remover” sites that ask you to upload a personal or client video without a clear privacy policy. Removing provenance or platform marks may also violate terms or disclosure expectations. A better approach is to choose a tool whose current plan allows the output you need and keep the original project files.

Common AI video problems and concrete fixes

Face changes between shots

Use one reference image when supported. Repeat the same hair, clothing, age range, lighting and camera distance. Avoid changing style words between scenes.

Hands look distorted

Reduce complex finger actions. Use “hands resting on desk” instead of “rapidly assembling a tiny device.” Crop wider if hands are not central to the story.

Objects flicker or transform

Ask for one slow action and a stable camera. Remove extra moving objects from the prompt. Image-to-video often helps when a product or vehicle must stay consistent.

Lip-sync feels wrong

Do not force a long spoken paragraph into a short generated shot. Create the voice first, use a dedicated lip-sync feature if available, or cut away to B-roll while narration continues.

Video feels boring

Change framing, not just subject. Alternate wide, medium and close shots. Put the strongest visual in the first two seconds and remove pauses before the first line.

Free credits disappear too fast

Storyboard before generating. Test prompts at the cheapest eligible setting, then spend higher-quality credits only on shots you know you need.

How this guide was tested and verified

For this update, Xenors checked official product/help pages for Google Flow, Adobe Firefly, Runway, Pika, Canva, Microsoft Clipchamp and YouTube on November 7, 2026. We compared their published free-access, credit, watermark, resolution or usage notes where those details were explicitly documented. We did not run paid generations across every tool or claim that one model produces the “best” video. Where an official source did not clearly verify a free-plan detail, this page tells you to check the current product page instead of guessing.

This article is educational. Before publishing commercial work, review the current terms for the tool, the rights to your input media, music and voice, and the disclosure rules of the platform where you upload.

Next step

Start with one 30-second video, not a full channel automation system. Write six scenes, generate only the shots you need, edit them into one coherent story and publish the result with the right AI disclosure. Once you know which part takes the most time—script, consistency, voice or editing—you can improve that specific step instead of adding more tools.
